newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore electronics fall might trim GDP forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Singapore electronics fall might trim GDP forecasts.

text.p: A 10.9 percent plunge in Singapore's January electronics output has some economists considering lowering their first quarter gross domestic product (GDP) forecasts.
On Wednesday, the Economic Development Board said manufacturing production fell 7.2 percent in January compared to a year ago, dragged down by a 10.9 percent drop in electronics.

"I'm not surprised there was weakness in electronics but the extent was a bit of a surprise. The impact on GDP is going to be felt in the first quarter. We probably need to look at the GDP numbers again," Ng Bok Eng, regional economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said on Thursday.
The electronics sector makes up about 25 percent of Singapore's GDP.
For first quarter year-on-year growth, "we have it as five percent...but most likely there would be some downward revision," Ng said.
Liew Yin Sze, chief economist at J.M. Sassoon, said the poorer-than-expected electronics number has prompted him to keep a close watch on economic data for February and March.

"It was worse than expected. It is not good news," Liew said. Referring to January export figures released earlier, he said: "Non-oil fell three percent. We had expected the numbers to be around there" in the industrial production report.
Singapore's non-oil domestic exports slipped 3.1 percent in January year-on-year.

"We shouldn't make too much of one month but at the same time it is one-third of a quarter. If the other two-thirds don't show any improvement, it will probably lead to some downward adjustment for first quarter GDP," said Liew, whose current forecast for first quarter growth is 5.6 percent.

P.K. Basu, director of regional economics at UBS Securities, said he was not surprised by the steep electronics fall because of a high base in the same period last year. But he was looking out for leading indicators of global electronics orders for a better indication of Singapore's economic recovery.
"If I see further dips in global order flows that would clearly put out the red flag for me," Basu said.

He said global orders for electronic components like semiconductors had not been particularly strong in November and December. Such indicators usually led Singapore's real exports by between four and six months.

"If that continues to turn down, it will prompt me to re-look at my forecasts," Basu said. He said he did not expect to revise his first quarter GDP projections of five percent but could lower his second quarter forecast from 6.8 percent if indicators didn't show signs of recovery.
Economists generally still expected Singapore's electronics and manufacturing sectors to start posting positive growth rates from the second quarter.
"The key is not whether recovery will come or not. What is important is if recovery will meet expectations," said Ng of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
He said his current expectation was for industrial production to grow seven percent for the year.
